In 1842 he gave the theory of *reducing a quadratic form to its principal axes by successive linear substitutions* \cite{jacobi1842} — the “Jacobi rotations” that, in various descendants, are still the workhorse behind computing eigenvalues and the SVD today. The published rotation method is Jacobi's 1846 paper in Crelle's Journal 30 (pp. 51–94); 1842 is not the date of the algorithm (\cite[Jacobi, 1846]{jacobi1846}).}
blocks.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

blocks.quote: Two facts turn the picture into engineering:
blocks.section: The SVD: the shape of any linear map

blocks.quote: That is why the SVD appears across this course under different names. **PCA** is the singular vectors of the data matrix, ordered by the variance they explain. **Low-rank compression** is “keep the top singular values.” **LoRA** fine-tunes a weight matrix by learning only a *low-rank* correction $\Delta W = BA$ \cite{hu2021lora} — the bet that the useful change lives in a few directions. And a layer’s “effective rank” (how fast its singular values decay) proxies how much of its capacity it actually uses. Applied to an attention head, the same “keep the top singular directions” idea becomes an interpretability tool: an SVD of a head’s query–key or value–output matrix isolates the one or two directions that carry the real signal when that head talks to a head several layers later — the **communication channels** that can be read straight off the weights (\cite[Merullo et al., 2024]{merullo2024talkingheads}) (see [Mechanistic Interpretability](mechanistic_interpretability)). See [Beyond LLMs](beyond_llms) for PCA and factorisation as algorithms.

blocks.quote: Descent: why the gradient is steepest
blocks.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

blocks.quote: Strictly, Cauchy's 1847 note treats simultaneous equations by minimising a sum of squares; it is not a general nonlinear-descent method. The name "steepest descent" and the convergence theory came later, with Hadamard's 1907–08 method (\cite[Hadamard, 1908]{hadamard1908}) and the mid-20th-century optimisation literature. The constrained version — project the gradient back onto the feasible set — is Rosen's gradient-projection method (1960) (\cite[Rosen, 1960]{rosen1960}), the direct ancestor of the projection step in modern constrained optimisers.
blocks.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

blocks.quote: \marginfig{cauchy.jpg}{Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1789–1857). In 1847 he proposed moving a point *against the gradient* to solve systems of equations and to fit by least squares \cite{cauchy1847} — the move later christened the **method of steepest descent**, and the same move every gradient-based optimizer makes on a loss landscape.}
blocks.section: Descent: why the gradient is steepest

blocks.quote: The *schedule* on top of this fact — momentum, Adam, learning-rate decay — is optimization, not geometry, covered in [The Optimizer](optimizerlab) and [Automatic Differentiation](autodiff). What we keep here: **the gradient is the normal to the level sets, and the steepest way down is to follow it.** In the interactive, drag the point around an oval bowl and watch the descent arrow (−∇) stay perpendicular to the contours; drag the valley narrow and it starts pointing across.

blocks.quote: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape
blocks.section: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape

blocks.quote: \marginfig{fourier.jpg}{Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier (1768–1830). In his 1822 *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* he argued that any signal is a sum of sines \cite{fourier1822} — the Fourier idea that makes the next paragraph possible. Fourier's claim was about functions (heat distributions), not "signals", and it was not a proof for arbitrary functions: convergence conditions were clarified later, notably by Dirichlet in 1829.}
blocks.section: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape

blocks.quote: The idea that a vibrating string is a sum of simple modes is older than Fourier. D'Alembert solved the one-dimensional wave equation in 1747 and wrote the solution as two travelling waves (\cite[d'Alembert, 1747]{dalembert1747}); contemporaries such as Daniel Bernoulli argued for the sine-series superposition, and Fourier's 1807 memoir on heat — expanded into the 1822 *Théorie* — made the general claim (\cite[Fourier, 1822]{fourier1822}).
blocks.section: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape

blocks.quote: The payoff is the **Fourier transform** $\mathcal{F}$ — a *change of coordinates*. It sends a signal to the list of sine-wave ingredients that build it. Write the signal and kernel in the basis of pure sine waves (“frequency” coordinates) instead of time. In that system the sliding sum becomes **ordinary multiplication**, point by point,
blocks.section: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape

blocks.quote: Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency \cite{fourier1822}. The reason: the sines are the directions in which the *slide* is normal. Shifting a sine in time only rotates its phase, so in the sine basis a shift is a rotation, and a sliding dot product of rotations is a product. The DFT finds those directions; the FFT is the fast way to compute them \cite{cooley1965fft}.
blocks.section: Convolution is a sliding dot product — the DFT is its shape

blocks.quote: This is not a curiosity. “Smooth the signal” means multiply its spectrum by a low-pass; “detect an edge” means the output lights up at high frequency; “a periodic hum” means energy piled up at one frequency. In audio the short-time Fourier view of sound is this identity (see [Speech & Audio](speech_audio)); in vision it underlies frequency filtering and the DFT tricks behind positional encoding and grokking (see [Positional Embeddings](positionalembeddingslab) and [The Shape of Space](geometry_i)). The two interactives share one kernel: drag its three taps and the time-domain output smooths (left) while the frequency-domain reason — pointwise multiplication — appears at the same time (right).

blocks.quote: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: Write the equivariance condition as a diagram that **commutes**: do the symmetry first, then the function, or the function first, then the symmetry — both paths land on the same point.
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: The modern definition is Klein's. In the *Erlangen Programme* of 1872 he proposed that a geometry *is* the study of what a group of transformations leaves invariant (\cite[Klein, 1872]{klein1872erlangen}). Read backwards, that is the neural-network question: choose the group — translations, permutations, rotations — and the architecture is the family of functions that respect it. Noether's 1918 theorem is the physicist's cousin: every continuous symmetry of an action yields a conserved quantity (\cite[Noether, 1918]{noether1918}). Weyl's *Classical Groups* (1939) catalogued the invariants themselves (\cite[Weyl, 1939]{weyl1939classicalgroups}).
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: These are not exotic — they are *forced*. **Deep Sets** \cite{zaheer2017deepsets} proved that any function of a *set* of inputs that is permutation-invariant must factor as “map each item, add them up, then pool”:
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: and it gives the matching condition for equivariance. “Map, sum, pool” is not a design choice — it is *the* shape any invariant or equivariant function on a set must have.
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: The theorem's hypothesis matters: for a countable universe the sum decomposition is exact; for uncountable domains the paper proves it only for sets of fixed size and conjectures the general case (\cite[Zaheer et al., 2017]{zaheer2017deepsets}). The equivariant form is different: for a linear layer it forces weight sharing, $\Theta=\lambda I+\gamma\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}$.
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: This matters because **weight sharing is equivariance in disguise**, and attention is *permutation-equivariant* rather than symmetric:
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: The interactive holds a bag of six “tokens.” Drag the **shift** to reorder them. The blue (input) and orange (per-item equivariant output) traces rotate *together* — equivariance, the commutative square closing. The flat green line is the invariant readout (the mean), which does not move no matter how you reorder.
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: > **A geometry is a group.** Klein (1872) defined a geometry by the transformations it leaves invariant; Noether (1918) turned continuous symmetry into conservation laws; Weyl (1939) catalogued the invariants. A CNN, a pooling layer and a GNN are three answers to Klein's question, written in weights.
blocks.section: Symmetry: invariance, equivariance, and the shape of attention

blocks.quote: Six “tokens” (a bag). Drag shift to cyclically reorder them. The blue trace is the reordered input and the orange trace is a fixed per-item function of it — an equivariant output, so the two move together. The flat green line is the invariant readout (the mean), which does not move for any reorder. The grey trace is the original order, for reference.

blocks.section: Synthesis: one forward pass, as geometry

blocks.quote: Notice what is *learned* and what is *fixed*. The geometry — a dot product measures alignment, the best fit is a shadow, the steepest direction is the normal to the level sets, convolution multiplies in frequency, a symmetric operation commutes with its symmetry — is **fixed by mathematics**. Training learns only the *parameters inside* each move: which directions to stretch, which kernel to slide, which per-item map to apply. The shape of the operations is a prior; the data supplies the numbers.
blocks.section: Synthesis: one forward pass, as geometry

blocks.quote: That is why the picture transfers. The same inner product that measures a neuron’s alignment measures a word’s similarity. The same projection that fits a line explains a low-rank approximation. The same SVD that shapes a matrix ranks a layer’s capacity. The same symmetry that justifies a shared filter is the reason attention needs position. A network is not “matrices of weights” but **geometry — points, shadows, stretches, level sets, sliding alignments, and symmetries** — and its layers become a single, navigable space.
blocks.section: Synthesis: one forward pass, as geometry
